entries.text: APPARAT CRITIQUE COMPARATIF [F] — X.16. La clôture du traité oppose machines offensives et ressources défensives à travers des exempla d’ingéniosité, de ruse technique et d’adaptation au site. Le caractère narratif de ces épisodes est conservé sans les transformer en prescriptions militaires modernes.SYNTHÈSE ECDOTIQUE — CLÔTURE DU LIVRE X. La révision de X est complète, de machina et des systèmes de levage à l’hydraulique, l’artillerie et la poliorcétique. Les zones de risque maximal sont identifiées : nombres, fractions, suppléments, vocabulaire grec, noms de pièces et reconstructions dépendantes des figures.SYNTHÈSE POUR LES ARCHITECTES [T] — LIVRE X. Vitruve réunit statique pratique, transmission du mouvement, hydraulique, instrumentation, torsion et construction de grands dispositifs dans la discipline de l’architectus. L’édition maintient distincts texte antique, explication mécanique et formalisation ingénierique moderne.

entries.anchor: PRONAOS [πρόναος]. Le porche ou vestibule d’entrée du temple, devant la cellule (cella).
entries.text: Le terme « pronaos », issu du grec ancien « ὁ πρόναος » (ho prónaos), se traduit littéralement par « devant le naos ». Ce terme est passé en latin sous la forme pronaon, du grec πρόναος, et signifie essentiellement « situé devant (pro) le temple (naós) ». Autrement dit, le pronaos est l’espace architectural situé devant le naos ou la cella du temple, et constitue un élément caractéristique des temples grecs et romains. Cet espace forme le vestibule ou l’entrée du temple et a généralement la même largeur que le naos, s’étendant dans le même axe.

entries.anchor: Gnomon (γνώμων) — gnomon. 9.7 : la tige qui projette l’ombre sur le cadran solaire, dont l’ombre (aussi σκιάθηρας) est lue contre l’analemme.
entries.text: ad normam : « à l’équerre ». La norma (γνώμων) est l’équerre du constructeur ; le terme reparaît au sens technique en 7.3.5. L’équivalence hauteur = envergure des bras (homo quadratus) fonde la théorie des proportions des temples qui suit.

entries.anchor: According to tradition, Vitruvius served as a military engineer under Julius Caesar, most likely during the Gallic Wars (c. 58–51 BCE). After retiring from military service, he dedicated himself to civil architecture and engineering. During this period, he built the only building he explicitly claims as his own work, the Basilica of Fanum Fortunae (modern-day Fano, in the Marche region of Italy), described in detail
entries.text: The basilica described by Vitruvius at Fanum Fortunae (Fano) must be distinguished from other Augustan basilicas excavated in Italy. Fanum denotes a consecrated place or sanctuary; fanaticus originally describes a person inspired by, or associated with, a sanctuary, before acquiring later pejorative senses. Profanus is formed from pro and fanum and denotes what lies before or outside the consecrated space; hence ‘profane’.

entries.anchor: Vitruvius was inspired by Hellenistic theorists to create his work, in which he makes explicit reference to the inventions of Ctesibius. "De architectura" addresses a wide range of topics, including architectural orders, materials, decorative techniques, construction, building typologies, hydraulics, colors, mechanics, and gnomonics (dealing with gnomonics in detail in Book IX).
entries.text: Ctesibius (Greek Κτησίβιος, Ktēsibios), active in the third century BCE, was an inventor and hydraulic and mechanical engineer associated with Alexandria. The ancient tradition credits him with important work on pneumatics, water pumps and improvements to the clepsydra. His investigations of compressed air and hydraulic devices hold a prominent place in the history of Hellenistic mechanics.

entries.anchor: Vitruvius was inspired by Hellenistic theorists to create his work, in which he makes explicit reference to the inventions of Ctesibius. "De architectura" addresses a wide range of topics, including architectural orders, materials, decorative techniques, construction, building typologies, hydraulics, colors, mechanics, and gnomonics (dealing with gnomonics in detail in Book IX).
entries.text: Gnomonics is the art and science of constructing and interpreting sundials. The term derives from Greek γνώμων (gnōmōn), which can denote an instrument or rod whose shadow allows a direction or a measure of time to be determined.

entries.anchor: Although the decisive discovery of the codex is attributed to Poggio Bracciolini (St. Gallen, 1416), humanist interest in Vitruvius had already been fostered by Petrarch; after the dissemination of the works of this Florentine, it can be said that Vitruvius became one of the principal textual sources for Renaissance architectural theory. The images that accompany Vitruvius's work in its editions up to the 18th centur
entries.text: Francesco Petrarca (born in Arezzo on July 20, 1304, and died in Arquà Petrarca on July 19, 1374) was a prominent poet, philosopher, and philologist from Arezzo. He is recognized as the father of humanism and a fundamental pillar of Italian literature, especially thanks to his work "Canzoniere" (Songbook). His poetry gave rise to a literary movement known as Petrarchism, which influenced prominent authors such as Garcilaso de la Vega in Spain, and in England, literary figures of the stature of William Shakespeare and Edmund Spenser. Beyond his influence on new forms and themes in poetry, Petrarch also promoted a humanist conception that sought to harmonize the heritage of ancient Greco-Roman culture with the principles of Christianity. Furthermore, he advocated for the unification of all Italian territories with the aim of restoring the region's former glory during the Roman Empire. His legacy endures as an iconic figure in the history of literature and humanist thought.

entries.anchor: "The Ten Books on Architecture" represents the most copied and translated classical treatise on architecture in history. One of the seminal texts of the Italian Renaissance, it has come down to us as a compendium of ancient knowledge and, according to Vitruvius, is also the first Latin treatise that aimed to provide a comprehensive exposition of architecture and the state of knowledge in civil engineering at the time
entries.text: Augustus, born Gaius Octavius in 63 BCE, was the first Roman emperor. Adopted by Julius Caesar in his will, he assumed Caesar’s name after 44 BCE; modern historians commonly call him Octavian for the period before he received the title Augustus from the Senate in 27 BCE. In Greek sources Καῖσαρ (Kaisar) corresponds to Latin Caesar.

entries.anchor: Regarding the architect's education, Vitruvius argues that their knowledge stems from the combination of two elements: "fabrica" (practical skill) and "ratiocinatio" (intellectual reasoning). This combination allows the architect to judge and understand all other trades. In the Renaissance, this distinction encouraged architects to break with medieval traditions and the builders' guild, allowing for a separation betw
entries.text: Leon Battista Alberti (born in Genoa, Italy, on February 18, 1404, and died in Rome on April 25, 1472) was a prominent architect, personal secretary (apostolic abbreviator) to three popes (Eugene IV, Nicholas V, and Pius II), and distinguished as an Italian humanist, writer, mathematician, and poet. His skills and contributions were not limited to these disciplines, as he also excelled as a cryptographer, linguist, philosopher, musician, and archaeologist. Alberti stands out as one of the most versatile and influential humanists of the Renaissance, and his legacy spans a wide range of fields of knowledge.

entries.anchor: For the theoretical training of the architect, Vitruvius advocated an education in the liberal arts, transferring the need for a well-rounded education from Cicero's rhetoric to his own field. This relates to the need for a complete education championed by the Greeks (called "enkykliospaideia"). entries.text: Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE) was a Roman orator, statesman, philosopher and author. His prose is a central point of reference for the Latin of the late Republic.

entries.anchor: According to current research, "The Ten Books on Architecture" offers the oldest and most comprehensive treatment of a wide range of subjects, including ancient technology, timekeeping, construction machinery, waterwheels, war machines, architecture, and interior design. This work comprehensively covers all aspects of construction and technology of the period. Before its publication, only brief compendiums and treati
entries.text: Hermogenes of Alabanda (Ἑρμογένης) was a Greek architect associated with Alabanda in Caria. Vitruvius connects him with the development of the pseudodipteral temple and with a preference for the Ionic over the Doric order. Among the works traditionally attributed to him are the temple of Artemis at Magnesia on the Maeander and the temple of Dionysus at Teos.

entries.anchor: Vitruvius achieved great fame in later periods, especially during the Renaissance. During this time, a new architectural style that took Antiquity as its model turned to Vitruvius to learn the fundamentals of Roman architecture. Searches were made for manuscripts of Vitruvius in monastic libraries, such as the one at Poggio Bracciolini. In 1511, Fra Giovanni Giocondo da Verona published another edition in Venice, and
entries.text: Cesare Cesariano (born ca. 1477 in Milan; died 30 March 1543) was an Italian painter, architect, and military engineer. In 1521 he published the first Italian translation of Vitruvius, to which he added a commentary and woodcut illustrations.

entries.anchor: A central passage in Vitruvius's treatise introduces the theory of the "well-formed man" (homo bene figuratus). The proportions of people in relation to one another are described using geometric shapes. This inspired sketches by several Renaissance artists, including Albrecht Dürer of Nuremberg, Mariano di Jacopo Taccola, Pellegrino Prisciani, and Francesco di Giorgio Martini. The most famous illustration comes from
entries.text: The formulas homo ad quadratum and homo ad circulum, commonly used in specialized literature, belong to the Renaissance interpretative tradition (Cesariano, Leonardo). Vitruvius (3.1.3) describes the proportions of the body inscribed in the circle and the square, but he does not use these Latin expressions as such; they are retained here for their conventional value.

entries.anchor: "De architectura" (also known as "Ten Books on Architecture, " De architectura libri decem) is a treatise written by the Roman architect and military engineer Marcus Vitruvius Pollio; c. 80–70 BCE – d. after 15 BCE. This work is dedicated to his patron, Emperor Caesar Augustus, and his sister Octavia Minor, to whose commendation Vitruvius attributes his introduction to the emperor. entries.text: The term "scriptorium," which literally means "a place for writing," is commonly used to refer to the designated room or space in medieval European monasteries where monastic scribes copied and transcribed manuscripts. These scriptoria were important centers of book production in the Middle Ages, where knowledge was preserved and transmitted through the copying of ancient texts and the creation of new manuscripts. Monastic scribes played a crucial role in the preservation and dissemination of literature, religion, and knowledge during that historical period.

entries.text: Giovanni Boccaccio (pronounced [d ͡ʒoˈ van ːi boˈkːat͡ʃː o]) was born on June 16, 1313, in Certaldo, Florence, and died on December 21, 1375, in Certaldo. He was a prominent Italian writer and poet, as well as a major figure in the humanism of the early Renaissance. His most famous work is the "Decameron," a collection of one hundred short stories that portrays the diverse society of the 14th century. This work established him as a founder of the prose narrative tradition in Europe. Boccaccio is known for his significant contribution to the literature and culture of his time, and his influence continues to resonate throughout the history of Italian and European literature.

entries.anchor: Little is known of Vitruvius’s life beyond his own account. His service with military engines is attested in the dedication, but identification of his precise office as praefectus fabrum remains a historical hypothesis. The title means “prefect of the craftsmen”; its correct form does not prove that Vitruvius held the appointment.
entries.text: Fabrum is the genitive plural of faber, ‘craftsman’ or ‘workman’; praefectus fabrum means ‘prefect of the craftsmen/workmen’, although the office’s precise function depends on its historical setting. Latin forms require morphological analysis before translation and should not be treated as isolated lexical equivalents.

entries.text: The Tetractys (Τετρακτύς in Greek) or Tetorakutes is a triangular figure consisting of ten dots arranged in four rows, with one, two, three, and four dots in each row. entries.text: Ad Quadratum is a constructive method that relates geometry to architecture within a system of proportions. In the design of Gothic cathedrals and religious temples, it was used as the foundation and framework of human geometry. It represents a state of consciousness and the achievement of squaring the circle.

entries.anchor: When we speak of the “divine proportion,” we are referring to a numerical relationship of spaces and a way of articulating geometries. It involves cutting a line into two unequal parts, such that the larger segment is to the whole line as the smaller is to the larger. In this way, a relationship of sizes is established, with the same proportionality between the whole divided into larger and smaller parts.

entries.anchor: According to the oldest surviving treatise on architecture, " De architectura, " or the 10 books of architecture by Vitruvius, 1st century BC, inspired by Hellenistic theorists, architecture rests on three principles: Beauty (venustas), Firmness (firmitas), and Utility (utilitas), or the wise organization of spaces.
entries.text: Firmitas, utilitas and venustas are the technical terms of De architectura 1.3.2. Modern reception often renders them ‘solidity, utility and beauty’, but Vitruvius defines them through foundations and materials, an arrangement suited to use, and the proportional correspondence of a building’s members.

entries.anchor: One of the characteristics common to the three Greek orders is entasis: the columns are slightly wider at the base and gradually narrow imperceptibly towards the capital, giving the column an organic elegance and vitality, avoiding the visual rigidity of a perfect cylindrical shape.
entries.text: Doric, Ionic and Corinthian forms belong to the Greek architectural tradition discussed by Vitruvius. His Tuscan arrangements are treated at 4.7. entries.text: Callimachus (Ancient Greek: Καλλίμαχος) (310 BC – 240 BC) was a poet and scholar, born in Cyrene and descended from a noble family. He was commissioned by Ptolemy II to organize the Library of Alexandria, a task he carried out until his death. His work was so significant that he is considered the father of librarians (or at least of catalogers). His Pinakes (Tablets), 120 volumes containing the complete catalog of the Library arranged chronologically, were of enormous value to subsequent bibliographic and literary studies of the Classical period.

entries.text: Ovid’s Metamorphoses is a Latin poem in fifteen books recounting transformations from the world’s beginnings to the deification of Julius Caesar. The Greek word μεταμόρφωσις means ‘transformation’; it is a Greek expression, not a Latin transcription. The poem was completed around 8 CE and exerted a lasting influence on later European literature and art.

entries.text: In Greek mythology, Peneus (Greek: Πηνειός) was a river god and one of the three thousand rivers. He was the son of Oceanus and Tethys. With the nymph Creusa, he had four children, including Hypseus, king of the Lapiths, and three daughters: Cyrene, Daphne, and Stilbe. However, according to other sources, Cyrene is considered one of his wives. Stilbe bore twin sons to the sun god Apollo: Centaurs and Lapith, the latter being the namesake of the Lapith people. Eros, the Greek god of love, shot an arrow at Apollo so that he would fall in love with Peneus's daughter, Daphne. According to the myth, Eros's purpose was for Daphne to scorn Apollo, as revenge for Apollo's mockery of her skill with the bow. Consequently, Daphne implored Peneus, the river god, for help, and he transformed her into a laurel tree, which from that moment on would be sacred to Apollo. In an Arcadian version of the myth, Daphne was the daughter of the god Ladon.

The canon is flexible, and the metric adapts to the requirements of the Aedes Augusti.

entries.text: Fra Giovanni Giocondo (born around 1433 in Verona and died in 1515) was a prominent Italian figure who played multiple roles throughout his life. Initially a religious figure and teacher, he distinguished himself especially as a scholar dedicated to the study of classical antiquity. Over time, he broadened his interests and became an eminent antiquarian, archaeologist, military engineer, and architect. His most notable legacy lies in being one of the first printers of Vitruvius's "De architectura," contributing significantly to the preservation and dissemination of this fundamental work.

entries.text: Ballista, related to Greek βάλλειν (‘to throw’), denotes an ancient two-armed torsion engine. Vitruvius distinguishes its calibration from that of the catapulta or scorpio: in 10.10 the initial datum is the length of the projectile, whereas in 10.11 the ballista is calibrated from the weight of the stone. The two systems must not be merged into a single modular rule.

entries.anchor: The transition from Vitruvius to Alberti: Leon Battista Alberti did not simply copy Vitruvius; he effected a subtle theoretical transmutation. While the Roman presented an eminently practical vision linked to state engineers, Alberti elevated venustas to the category of Concinnitas (the universal harmony of all parts regulated by absolute mathematical laws, where nothing can be altered without destroying the whole).
entries.text: De re aedificatoria (‘On the Art of Building’) is Leon Battista Alberti’s Latin architectural treatise in ten books, composed around the middle of the fifteenth century. Its critical engagement with Vitruvius made it a foundational text of Renaissance architectural theory.

entries.text: The Tuscan arrangement described by Vitruvius at 4.7 derives from the Etrusco-Italic temple: a column with a simple base, an unfluted shaft and an undecorated capital, with robust proportions. Renaissance theorists, including Serlio, Vignola and Palladio, codified it as the first and simplest of the architectural orders.

entries.text: In Vitruvius (9.1.1; 9.7), the analemma (ἀνάλημμα) is a geometrical projection used to lay out a sundial’s hour lines. It is distinct from the figure-of-eight curve also called an analemma in modern astronomy.

entries.text: A clepsydra (from the Greek κλεψύδρα, kléptein,"To steal, and ὕδωρ hydōr," water") is any mechanism for measuring time by the regulated flow of a liquid into or out of a graduated container, thus giving rise to two different types of clocks depending on the direction of the flow. Clepsydras date back to ancient Egypt (mrḫyt) and were used especially at night, when sundials were no longer useful. The earliest water clocks consisted of a ceramic vessel filled with water to a certain level, with a hole at the base of a suitable size to ensure the liquid flowed out at a specific rate and, therefore, in a predetermined time. The container had several markings inside, so that the water level indicated the different periods, both day and night.

entries.text: Ctesibius (Κτησίβιος), active in third-century BCE Alexandria, was an inventor and hydraulic and mechanical engineer. entries.text: Caryatids are sculpted female figures that replace columns as supports for an entablature; the canonical example is the porch of the Erechtheion on the Acropolis at Athens (c. 421–406 BC). In 1.1.5 Vitruvius offers an aetiological explanation intended to show why architects must know history: the women of Caryae, a town in Laconia that sided with Persia, were supposedly enslaved and their images condemned to bear the weight of a building for ever. The story is now regarded as a late aetiological construction rather than the actual origin of the motif, which scholarship associates instead with archaic korai and the cult of Artemis Caryatis, whose ritual dances were performed by the girls of Caryae.

entries.text: Ctesibius (Greek Κτησίβιος) was a Greek inventor, hydraulic engineer and mathematician associated with Alexandria in the third century BC. Ctesibius was especially important for Hellenistic hydraulics and mechanical invention. The dates 285–222 BC should not be used as secure birth and death dates without independent evidence; the chronology of Ctesibius and that of Archimedes must not be conflated. Compare the Aquincum Museum’s account, “Ctesibius: The barber of Alexandria”, which places his activity in the early third century BC.

entries.text: Philolaus, also known as Philolaus of Tarentum or of Croton (Greek Φιλόλαος, Philolaos; c. 470–c. 380 BC), was a Greek Pythagorean and Presocratic philosopher, mathematician, astronomer, politician, music theorist and writer. He held that all matter consists of limiting and unlimited things joined by harmony, and that the universe is determined by numbers. He is credited with originating the hypothesis that the Earth was not the center of the universe, a theory included in the Pythagorean astronomical system.

entries.anchor: “17. Those whom nature has endowed with such skill, intellectual acuity and memory that they thoroughly master geometry, astronomy, music and the other disciplines go beyond the duties of architects and become mathematicians. They can readily discuss these disciplines, armed as they are with many intellectual weapons. Such people are rare: among them were Aristarchus of Samos, Philolaus and Archytas of Tarentum, Apol
entries.text: Apollonius of Perga, also called Perge (Greek Ἀπολλώνιος; c. 262 BC–Alexandria, c. 190 BC), was a Greek mathematician and astronomer renowned for his work on conic sections. He gave the names ellipse, parabola and hyperbola to the curves now known by those terms. His study of conic sections informed later geometrical problem-solving; it should not be equated uncritically with the symbolic solution of general quadratic equations in modern algebra.

entries.anchor: « 2. Order is the balanced adjustment of the individual members of the work taken separately, and, for the work as a whole, the comparison of the proportion with a view to a symmetrical result. It is composed of quantity, which in Greek is called ποσότης. Quantity, in turn, consists in taking the modules from the members of the work itself and, from the several parts of those members, producing the harmonious and fit
entries.text: F. Arq. Delineation of the floor of a building.

entries.anchor: « 3. Eurythmy is a beautiful appearance and a graceful, becoming aspect in the composition of the members. This is achieved when the members of the work are of a height suited to their width, a width suited to their length, and, in sum, all correspond to their symmetry. »
entries.text: From the Latin eurythmia. Eurythmia refers to the act of moving in a harmonious way and seeking beauty.

entries.anchor: « 5. Decorum, in turn, is the faultless appearance of a work composed, with authority, of approved elements. It is achieved by prescription—which in Greek is called θεματισμός, by usage, or by nature. By prescription, when temples to Jupiter the Lightning-bringer, to the Heaven, the Sun, and the Moon are erected in the open air and unroofed (hypaethral); for of these gods we behold the semblance and the active power
entries.text: Vitruvius preserves some of his associations in the section of his work On Architecture in which he describes how the design of a temple (aedes) should reflect the nature of the deity that will be housed in it: The character of the Corinthian order seems most appropriate for Venus, Flora, Proserpina and the nymphs [ Lymphae ] of the Fountains; for its slenderness, elegance and richness, and its ornamental leaves topped by volutes, seem to bear analogy to their dispositions.

entries.anchor: “6. Propriety according to custom is achieved when magnificent interiors are accompanied by fitting and elegant vestibules. If the interiors offer elegant views but the entrances are low and undistinguished, the building will lack propriety. Likewise, if dentils are carved in the cornices of Doric entablatures, or triglyphs are introduced into Ionic entablatures with cushion-capital columns, the transfer of features
entries.text: A triglyph (Greek τρίγλυφος, from τρι-, “three”, and γλύφος, “carving” or “groove”) is a characteristic architectural ornament of the Doric frieze: a rectangular element in relief, taller than it is wide, with three vertical bands separated by two complete grooves and two half-grooves, one at each end. Sometimes only the central grooves occur.

entries.anchor: 1.4.1 But for the city walls themselves the governing principles will be these. First comes the choice of a thoroughly healthy site: one that is elevated, free from mist and frost, facing quarters of the sky that are neither sweltering nor cold but temperate, and, further, removed from the neighborhood of marshes. For when the morning breezes reach the town at sunrise, bringing with them the mists that have gathered
entries.text: This explanation belongs to ancient environmental medicine: Vitruvius links mist, marshes, exhalations and disease. The note preserves that historical reasoning without recasting it as knowledge of microorganisms.

entries.anchor: 1.4.5 Therefore, it seems that one must be careful in placing walls away from those regions that can spread hot winds to human bodies. For just as all bodies are composed of the principles that the Greeks call stoicheia, that is, of heat and moisture, of earth and air, so the qualities of all animals in the world are generally formed by natural mixtures of temperature.
entries.text: Στοιχεῖα (stoicheia) here means “elements” or “constituent principles”. Vitruvius enumerates heat, moisture, the earthy component and air within an ancient physical theory; these are not chemical elements in the modern sense.

entries.anchor: 1.5.2 Likewise, the towers must be projected beyond the outer face of the wall, so that when an enemy seeks to press an assault against it, he may be wounded by missiles from the towers on his right and left, his flanks lying exposed. Above all, care must be taken that there be no easy approach for storming the wall; rather, the ground about the towers should be so disposed that the way to the gates runs not straight
entries.text: Scaeva describes an oblique or skewed approach. Vitruvius’s explanation presupposes a shield carried on the left arm: the attacker’s right side is more exposed as he approaches the wall.

entries.anchor: 1.5.5 The towers, therefore, should be built round or polygonal; for siege-engines dismantle square towers the more readily, since the rams shatter the corners by their battering, whereas in rounded forms, driving the stones towards the center as if with wedges, they can do no harm. Likewise, fortifications of wall and towers joined with earthworks are by far the safest, since neither rams nor mining nor the other en
entries.text: The preference for circular or polygonal towers is explained within the siege technology known to Vitruvius, especially the impact of a battering ram on projecting corners. It is not a universal structural law.

entries.anchor: 1.6.2 Wind is a flowing wave of air with a certain excess of motion. It arises when heat meets moisture and the impulse generated in producing breath forces out the power of the blast. This can be observed in bronze aeolipiles, through ingenious devices that reveal the truth of the hidden workings of the heavens. Hollow bronze spheres are made with a very narrow opening, filled with water and set beside a fire. Befor
entries.text: The aeolipile is used here to demonstrate the action of heat on water and the resulting flow of air, in support of Vitruvius’s account of the winds (1.6.2).

entries.anchor: 1.6.4 Some have held that there are four winds: Solanus from the equinoctial east, Auster from the south, Favonius from the equinoctial west and Septentrio from the north. Those who investigated more carefully, however, stated that there are eight, notably Andronicus of Cyrrhus. As an example he erected an octagonal marble tower at Athens, with an image of each wind carved on the face corresponding to the direction f
entries.text: The so-called Tower of the Winds at Athens, attributed to Andronicus of Cyrrhus, is a Hellenistic octagonal building associated with representations of eight winds. Vitruvius uses it as material support for his anemological system.

entries.text: Vitruvius’s account of the winds (1.6) begins with eight principal winds, associated with Andronicus of Cyrrhus and the Tower of the Winds at Athens. Streets laid along the bisectors of the octants are intended to exclude direct currents from their axes. At 1.6.10 he adds sixteen subsidiary names to the eight principal winds, giving a twenty-four-wind scheme. Compare Aristotle, Meteorologica 2.6, and Pliny, Natural History 2.119–121.

entries.anchor: 1.6.6 Let a marble plane be set level in the center of the city, or let the ground be smoothed with a straightedge and level so that a marble plane is unnecessary. Place a bronze gnomon, a shadow-tracer, at its center. At about the fifth hour of the morning mark the tip of the gnomon’s shadow. With the compasses opened from the center to that mark, describe a circle. Then observe the growing shadow in the afternoon;
entries.text: Σκιαθήρας literally means “shadow hunter” or “shadow observer”. The procedure using morning and afternoon shadows of equal length establishes a meridian line without using a magnetic compass.

entries.anchor: 1.6.9 Perhaps those acquainted with many names of winds will be surprised that we have set down only eight. But if they observe that the circuit of the earth's globe, by the course of the sun, the shadows of the equinoctial gnomon, and the inclination of the heavens, was found by Eratosthenes of Cyrene through mathematical reckoning and geometrical method to be two hundred and fifty-two thousand stadia, which make th
entries.text: Eratosthenes of Cyrene (Greek Ἐρατοσθένης; born between 276 and 273 BC at Cyrene, died around 194 BC at Alexandria) was an exceptionally versatile Greek scholar at the height of Hellenistic science.

entries.text: Vitruvius attributes a circumference of 252,000 stadia for the Earth to Eratosthenes. Conversion into modern units depends on the length assigned to the stadium; the edition therefore retains the ancient value without imposing a single equivalent.

entries.anchor: 1.7.1 Once the lanes and streets have been laid out, sites must be chosen for sacred temples, the forum and other public places, with regard to the city’s convenience and common use. In a coastal town the forum should be near the harbour; in an inland town, at its center. Temples of the gods under whose special protection the city stands, such as Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, should occupy the highest place, from which
entries.text: Vitruvius presents the reasons for placing the temples of Venus, Vulcan and Mars outside the walls as prescriptions of the discipline of the Etruscan haruspices. They should be read as ancient religious rationalizations rather than secular zoning criteria.

entries.anchor: II.Pr.1 Dinocrates the architect, trusting in his ideas and ingenuity, left Macedonia for the army while Alexander was in power, eager to win the king’s favor. He brought letters from relatives and friends at home to the leading officers and courtiers, hoping to gain easier access. They received him kindly, and he asked to be brought before Alexander as soon as possible. Although they promised to do so, they delayed
entries.text: Dinocrates (Δεινοκράτης; transmitted forms Dinocrates and Deinochares) was a Greek architect contemporary with Alexander the Great. Vitruvius devotes the preface to Book II (2.pref.1–4) to him, recounting how he presented himself to the king and proposed carving Mount Athos into a colossal statue, with a city in its left hand and, in its right, a basin collecting the mountain’s waters and discharging them into the sea. Alexander rejected the project after asking about land capable of feeding the city, but retained its author. Tradition attributes to Dinocrates the plan of Alexandria, founded in 331 BC, and its orthogonal Hippodamian layout. His identification with the Chirocrates mentioned by Strabo remains disputed, as do the attribution of Hephaestion’s funeral pyre at Babylon and of work on the temple of Artemis at Ephesus. In Vitruvius the episode serves an argumentative purpose: it contrasts princely favor with professional competence alone and introduces the author’s vindication of his own position.

entries.anchor: II.Pr.2 The unusual sight drew the crowd’s attention, and Alexander saw him. Astonished, he ordered room to be made for him to approach and asked who he was. “Dinocrates,” he replied, “a Macedonian architect, bringing you ideas and designs worthy of your glory. I have designed Mount Athos in the form of a male statue: in its left hand I have represented the walls of a very large city, and in its right a patera, a rit
entries.text: The Athos project is discussed on the basis of Vitruvius’s account. The parallel ancient testimonies are not identical and should not be merged into a single biography of Dinocrates without indicating their differences.

entries.anchor: II.Pr.3 Delighted by the account of the design, Alexander immediately asked whether there was farmland nearby capable of supplying the city with grain. Learning that it could be sustained only by supplies brought from overseas, he said: “Dinocrates, I appreciate the excellence of your design and take pleasure in it, but anyone who founded a colony there would, I see, be criticized for his judgment. Just as a newborn
entries.text: Frumentaria ratio concerns the capacity to supply the population with grain. The comparison with an infant deprived of milk turns territorial food supply into a criterion for the viability of a city.

entries.anchor: 2.1.1 In the earliest ages of the world, men were born like the wild beasts in forests, caves, and groves, and passed their lives feeding upon wild fare. Meanwhile, in a certain place, trees densely crowded and tossed by storms and winds, and rubbing their branches one against another, kindled fire; and those who were about that place, terrified by the fierce flame, were put to flight. Afterwards, when it had grown q
entries.text: The origin of fire and language belongs to an ancient genealogy of civilisation. Parallels with Lucretius or other intellectual traditions are comparative; Vitruvius does not declare any precise doctrinal dependence here.

entries.anchor: 2.1.2 The discovery of fire thus first gave rise to gatherings, deliberation and communal life, and brought more people together in one place. Nature had given them an advantage over the other animals: they walked upright rather than bent towards the ground, could contemplate the magnificence of the world and stars, and could handle whatever they wished with their hands and fingers. In that gathering some began to ma
entries.text: Upright posture and manual skill form part of the ancient anthropology through which Vitruvius explains the origins of civic life (2.1.2).

Heraclitus of Ephesus, whom the Greeks called skoteinos (σκοτεινός) because of the obscurity of his writings, held fire to be that principle. entries.text: Heraclitus of Ephesus (Ἡράκλειτος ὁ Ἐφέσιος), active around the end of the sixth and beginning of the fifth century BCE, was a Presocratic philosopher from Ionia. His writings survive only in fragments and testimonia.

entries.anchor: 3. Now there are three kinds of bricks. One which is called Lydian in Greek, that is, which our people use, is a foot and a half long and a foot wide. With the other two Greek buildings are built. Of these one is called pentadoron, the other tetradoron. But the Greeks call doron a palm, because the giving of gifts is called doron in Greek, and this is always done with the palm of the hand. So that which is five palms
entries.text: Πεντάδωρον and τετράδωρον express modules of five and four palms. Modern metric equivalents depend on the standard adopted and must be identified as editorial conversions.

entries.anchor: Three kinds of bricks are made. The Lydian brick used by our people is a foot and a half long and one foot wide. The two other kinds are used in Greek buildings: pentadoron and tetradoron. The Greeks call the palm doron, associating it with the giving of gifts, which is done with the palm of the hand. A square brick of five palms on each side is pentadoron; one of four palms is tetradoron. Public buildings use the fo
entries.text: Both Vitruvius and Pliny mention three types of brick: Lydian, tetradoron and pentadoron (Adam 1996, 64; Cairoli 2004, 152; Vitruvius 1995, 103). So-called half-bricks were also manufactured. When the bricks are laid level, one above another, courses of full bricks alternate with courses of half-bricks (Vitruvius 1995, 104).

entries.anchor: 1. For rubble masonry, the first requirement is sand suitable for mixing mortar and free from earth. The kinds of pit sand are black, gray, red and carbunculus. The best sand makes a gritty sound when rubbed in the hand; sand mixed with earth lacks that roughness. If sand is thrown onto a white cloth and shaken off, leaving neither a stain nor a deposit of earth, it is suitable.
entries.text: Carbunculus/carbuncularis is a problematic ancient designation for a variety of sand; a modern geological identification not specified by the text is not imposed.

entries.anchor: 1. Having explained the supplies of sand, I must also discuss lime, which should be burned from white stone or silex. Lime from dense, harder stone is useful in masonry; lime from porous stone is useful in plaster. Once the lime has been slaked, mix the mortar in these proportions: three parts sand to one part lime when pit sand is used, or two parts sand to one part lime when river or sea sand is used. These give th
entries.text: The transmitted proportions are an ancient recipe rather than a contemporary standardized mortar specification.

This appears to happen because beneath those mountains lie hot earth and numerous springs, which could not exist without great subterra

entries.anchor: 4. To avoid this defect, leave the space behind the facing stones and build inner walls two feet thick of squared red stone, fired brick or ordinary hard stone. Tie the inner work to the outer faces with iron clamps secured with lead. Built in regular courses rather than loose heaps, the work can remain sound: the beds and bonded joints keep the masonry from thrusting out, while the connected facing stones prevent it
entries.text: orthostata, -ae] From Greek ὀρθοστάτης, “an upright element”. In building terminology it denotes a block or slab set vertically in the lower part of a wall facing. The note retains the technical term and avoids equating it without qualification with a modern “post”.

entries.anchor: Greek masonry should therefore not be disparaged. The Greeks do not make a carefully finished facing of soft rubble: when not using ashlar, they build with ordinary hard stone, laying it like brick and bonding the joints in alternating courses. They thus achieve lasting strength. They build this masonry in two forms, one called isodomon and the other pseudisodomon.
entries.text: isodomum / pseudoisodomum] From Greek ἰσόδομον / ψευδισόδομον. In opus isodomum the courses have a regular height; in pseudoisodomum courses of different heights alternate. The distinction concerns masonry bond and the modulation of courses, not the nature of the material.

entries.anchor: Another kind, called emplekton, is also used by our country builders. Its faces are dressed, while the stones within are left in their natural state and bonded with mortar in alternating courses. Our builders, pursuing speed, set the facings upright and fill the middle separately with rubble and mortar, producing three distinct layers: two outer faces and an inner filling. The Greeks instead lay their stones flat and
entries.text: In architecture and construction, masonry bond (Spanish aparejo, related to Latin apparare, “to prepare”; opus in descriptions of Roman building) is the form, structure or constructive arrangement of a wall.

entries.anchor: The house of Croesus, which the people of Sardis assigned to the citizens of their city to rest in the leisure of their age, to the college of elders. Likewise, the house of the most powerful king Mausolus at Halicarnassus, although it was adorned with Proconnesian marble, has walls built of brick, which for this time show excellent strength, so polished by the works of painting that they seem to have the translucenc
entries.text: Mausolus, son of Hecatomnus, was a ruler of Caria under Achaemenid authority. His building activity and the monument at Halicarnassus belong to the historical context of the architectural examples discussed here. Details of his youth and personal contacts require independent evidence.

entries.anchor: His judgment and skill in planning buildings may be understood as follows. Born at Mylasa, he observed that Halicarnassus offered natural defenses, a suitable trading center and a useful harbour, and established his residence there. The site curves like a theater. At its lowest part, beside the harbour, he laid out the forum; halfway up the curving slope he made a broad street, with the Mausoleum at its center, a wor
entries.text: Leochares /liːˈɒkəriːz/ (Greek: Λεοχάρης or Λεωχάρης) was an ancient Greek sculptor from Athens, who lived in the 4th century BC. Works: Leochares worked on the construction of the Mausoleum of Mausolus at Halicarnassus, one of the "Seven Wonders of the Ancient World." The Diana of Versailles is a Roman copy of his original (c. 325 BC). He is also believed to be the creator of the famous Apollo Belvedere, of which a Roman copy is currently kept in Vatican City. In Greek mythology, Salmacis was a Phrygian nymph who loved Hermaphroditus.

Would that nature had followed his judgment and made them manifest and visible! Then not only wo
entries.text: The Temple of Apollo, also known as the Apollonion (Greek: Ἀπολλώνιον, Romanized: Apollṓnion), was an important part of the pan-Hellenic religious sanctuary located in central Greece at Delphi. The temple and the sanctuary in general were dedicated to one of the major Greek deities, Apollo, the god of archery, music, light, prophecy, the arts, and healing.

entries.text: Polyclitus (Greek: Πολύκλειτος), called " the Elder " to distinguish him from Polyclitus the Younger, was a 5th-century BC Greek bronze sculptor born in Argos or Sicyon. Along with the famous Phidias, Myron, and Cresilas, he is one of the most important sculptors of classical antiquity. The 4th-century BC catalog attributed to Xenocrates (" Xenocratic Catalog "), which served as Pliny's guide to art, placed Polyclitus between Phidias and Myron. Polyclitus was most famous for his bronze statues of gods and athletes, apart from the enormous statue of the goddess Hera, intended for worship in the Heraion of Argos. One of his most outstanding sculptures is the Doryphoros.

entries.text: Ad normam means ‘to the square’. The norma (γνώμων) is the builder’s square; the term recurs technically at 7.3.5. The relation between bodily height and the span of the outstretched arms underlies the discussion of the homo quadratus and temple proportion.

entries.anchor: Likewise, the natural center of the body is the navel. For if a man be laid on his back, with his hands and feet outstretched, and the point of a compass be placed upon his navel, the circle thereby described will touch the tips of the fingers of both hands and of the toes. And just as the body yields a circular outline, so too a square figure may be found within it: for if the distance from the soles of the feet to
entries.text: The classic passage on inscribing the human body in geometrical figures (homo ad circulum et ad quadratum). This passage and the preceding one (3.1.2) gave rise to Leonardo da Vinci’s celebrated drawing (c. 1490, Gallerie dell’Accademia, Venice). Leonardo, however, does not inscribe the two figures concentrically, as is often assumed, but moves the center of the square to the pubis, departing from the letter of Vitruvius’s text. Compare 3.1.2–3 and Pliny, Natural History 7.77, on the body’s commensurability.

The width of the abacus, equal to the lower thickness of the column. Let the thickness of the capital be divided into three parts: one given to the plinth, which is on the abacu
entries.text: The term " plinth," derived from the Latin "plinthus" and, in turn, from the Greek "πλίνθος" meaning "brick," refers to the square-based molding found beneath the base of a column or pilaster, similar in shape to an abacus. This architectural element rests on the pedestal. When the pedestal extends continuously, a single plinth supports all the columns and is called a "stylobate." It is thought that its origin may be related to the stone that served as the base for the column or the wooden upright in ancient architecture.

entries.anchor: 3. Seeing also that the citizens were occupied with public and private affairs, I judged that I should write briefly, so that they could grasp my subject during their limited leisure. Pythagoras and the followers of his school likewise chose to set down their precepts in books on a cubic principle: they made one cube consist of 216 verses and thought that no more than three such units should appear in a single compos
entries.text: Vitruvius invokes cubic organization in the preface to Book V as a way of arranging a manageable body of knowledge. The interpretation of his name as an acronym developed in this work is the author’s hermeneutic proposal, rather than an established etymology or an independently documented explanation of the ancient title.

entries.anchor: 4. A cube is a solid bounded by equal square faces. When thrown, it remains stable on whichever face it rests, provided it is left untouched, like the dice cast by players into a gaming tray. The comparison seems to have been adopted because this number of verses, once established in the mind as a cube rests on a face, would give memory a similar stability. Greek comic poets also divided their plays by inserting song
entries.text: Vitruvius discusses six as a perfect number in Book III, chapter 1, and invokes the Pythagorean cube of six, 216, in the preface to Book V. The two passages concern different parts of his argument: bodily and numerical proportion in the former, the measured organization of technical writing in the latter.

entries.text: Vitruvius describes tuned bronze sounding vessels, vasa aerea or ἠχεῖα, in De architectura 5.5. The acoustic pots found in some medieval churches belong to a different historical and material context. Their intended function and any connection with Vitruvian practice require separate archaeological assessment.

entries.text: The account concerns Aristophanes of Byzantium (c. 257–180 BCE), the scholar associated with the Library of Alexandria. Vitruvius’s anecdote illustrates literary judgment and the condemnation of plagiarism; it should not relocate Aristophanes to Pergamum merely because that library figures elsewhere in the preface.

entries.anchor: [2] For what does Milo of Croton, who was undefeated, do to men or to others who were victors of that kind, except that, while they lived, they enjoyed nobility among their citizens? But the precepts of Pythagoras, the daily cultivation of Democritus, Plato, Aristotle, and other wise men by the constant industry, bear fresh and flourishing fruits not only to their own citizens, but also to all nations. From which tho
entries.text: Χειρόκμητα] The title associated with Democritus has a complex textual history. Krohn’s Vitruvian text prints χειρουμμετων; the form Χειρόκμητα draws on the parallel tradition and philological correction (compare Pliny, Natural History 24.160, and Diogenes Laertius 9.49). Χειρόκμητα is adopted here as an editorially normalized form, with that status made explicit.

entries.anchor: Among Archimedes’s many remarkable inventions, the one I shall now describe seems to show extraordinary ingenuity. When Hiero had acquired royal power at Syracuse and his affairs had prospered, he decided to dedicate a golden crown to the immortal gods in a temple. He contracted for its manufacture and weighed out the gold to the craftsman on a balance. The completed work was presented to the king at the appointed ti
entries.text: εὕρηκα εὕρηκα] Vitruvius transmits the exclamation in Greek in the account of Archimedes (9, preface 10–11 in this edition’s numbering). Krohn (1912) prints the Greek words. Their accents are normalized here; they are not presented as a modern conjecture replacing a Latin transliteration in the manuscripts.

entries.anchor: [1] These things are ordained by the divine mind and excite great wonder in those who consider that the shadow of the equinoctial gnomon is of one size in Athens, another in Alexandria, another in Rome, not the same in Placentia and other parts of the world. Therefore, they differ greatly from the descriptions of the clocks of places. For the sizes of the equinoctial shadows are designated by the forms of the analemm
entries.text: ἀνάλημμα] The Greek form is supplied editorially where the running Latin text gives analemma in Latin letters. This is a technical term of gnomonics, denoting the geometrical projection used in the construction of sundials.

Therefore, I will explain how this seems to be done. Its rays in the world are extended in the form of a triangle with equal sides, by lines. But this is neither more nor less than the fifth sign from that sign. Therefore, if the rays were to wander through
entries.text: καῖε τὰ πόρρω, τἀγγύθεν δ’ εὔκρατ’ ἔχει] A verse of Euripides (Phaethon, fr. 771 Nauck), supplied here in Greek by reference to the fragment’s parallel tradition. Editorial restitution is distinguished from the form transmitted in the Vitruvian witnesses.

entries.anchor: [1] A machine is a connected assemblage of timber, possessing the greatest powers for the moving of loads. It is set in motion by the art of circular movements, which the Greeks call cyclic movement. Of these there is one kind for scaling, which in Greek is called acrobaticon; another is a breathing machine, which among them is called a pneumatic; the third is the hoisting type (tractorium), which the Greeks call bar
entries.text: βαροῦλκον] At 10.1.1 Vitruvius uses this Greek term for the genus tractorium, the class of machines employed to draw or raise loads. Krohn (1912) prints the Greek word. It is retained and glossed as a traction or lifting apparatus, without claiming an independently verified restoration from a manuscript transliteration.

entries.anchor: [1] There follows the machine of Ctesibius, which raises water to a height. It is made of bronze. At its base are two cylinders (modioli) set a little apart, with pipes joined in the shape of a fork and meeting at a central vessel. In this vessel are fitted valves (asses), carefully placed over the upper mouths of the pipes, which by stopping those openings keep back what has been driven into the vessel under pressur
entries.text: The pump of Ctesibius described by Vitruvius (10.7) uses two bronze cylinders, pipes, valves and pistons operated by rods and levers to force water into a central vessel and an ascending pipe. This explanation follows the Vitruvian description; comparisons with later pumps belong to the history of technology rather than to the ancient text.

entries.anchor: 3. The cult of Janus (Ianus) and the architecture of transit [hermeneutic reading]
entries.text: Janus (Latin Ianus) is the Roman god of passages, doors and beginnings, represented with two faces. The month Ianuarius, from which English January and Spanish enero derive, was dedicated to him. He was invoked at the beginning of undertakings, at the start of the year and in rites associated with the opening and closing of war. He has no exactly corresponding Greek equivalent.

entries.anchor: Vitruvius prioritizes the ideal architect over the art of architecture, thus restricting access to the realm of architecture. The architect embodies architecture (a royal compendium of all things, united through art), but is only perfected through a comprehensive training course in various disciplines, which Vitruvius likens to a corpus. This discipline, the encyclios, has evoked the liberal arts for many readers, wh
entries.text: Encyclios is related to Greek ἐγκύκλιος, ‘circular’ or ‘general’, as in the expression ἐγκύκλιος παιδεία for a general education. In the present context it denotes the interconnected course of disciplines relevant to the architect’s formation.
